title: The Schlieffen Plan and the march to the Marne
subtitle: A timetable the world fell behind — August–November 1914
summary: Germany's war plan staked everything on beating France inside six weeks by a right-wing sweep through Belgium, before Russia could mobilize. This pack follows the five German armies from the Meuse to the Marne, the French Plan XVII offensive that walked into the German left, the British at Mons and Le Cateau, the Great Retreat, Joffre's redeployment by rail, the counterstroke of 5–12 September, and the four months' fighting from the Aisne to Ypres that ended in a continuous trench line from the North Sea to Switzerland. A hypothetical branch renders Schlieffen's concept — the wheel west of Paris — beside what actually happened.

headline: August 1914.
Germany has forty days.
opening.lede: The German plan is a bet about time: beat France in the west before Russia can bring her armies to bear in the east, by a right-wing sweep through Belgium. Everything that follows is that timetable meeting the ground.[^herwig-2009]

branches.title: What happened
branches.summary: The campaign as it was fought: the right wing thinned by detachments, Kluck's wheel inside Paris, the gap, the Marne, the Aisne.

branches.title: Schlieffen's concept
branches.summary: The sweep as the 1905 memorandum drew it, and nothing more: from 25 August the right wing keeps its weight, the 1st Army passes west of Paris, the 2nd inside it, the 3rd pins the centre, and the whole wheels south and east. A schematic rendering of an idea — the French armies are left where history put them, and no outcome is claimed. For what the idea would have needed to come true, open 'What success required'.
branches.historiography: Whether a 'Schlieffen Plan' existed as an operational plan is itself contested. Zuber argues that the December 1905 memorandum was a staff study and a plea for more divisions, and that 'the Schlieffen Plan' was constructed after 1918 by officers who needed a plan that Moltke had spoiled;[^zuber-2002] Mombauer, Holmes and Foley reply that Moltke inherited a real deployment concept and altered it — dropping the Netherlands, strengthening the left, planning the Liège coup.[^mombauer-2001] Herwig's narrative treats the memorandum's geometry as the yardstick the campaign was measured against by the men who fought it.[^herwig-2009] This branch draws the geometry; it takes no side on whether it was ever a plan.

branches.title: What success required
branches.summary: The envelopment as it would have had to happen for the war in the West to be won in six weeks: the right wing at full weight passes west of Paris, wheels behind the French left, and with the centre pinning and the Metz hinge holding closes a pocket against the Verdun–Toul–Épinal fortress line; the BEF is pushed out of the battle to the south-west and the French 5th, 4th and 9th Armies are caught between the Seine and the fortresses. Presented as an argument, not a fantasy: the checklist below lists what would have had to be true, and marks what actually was.
branches.historiography: Could the sweep ever have worked? Herwig does the arithmetic of the outer wheel — march rates the 1st Army could not have bettered, supply days behind the railheads, corps that had in fact gone elsewhere — and is sceptical;[^herwig-2009] Strachan treats the plan as beyond the means of the army that was asked to execute it, and the 'six weeks' as a hope rather than a calculation;[^strachan-2001] Zuber goes further and denies there was a plan to fail;[^zuber-2002] Mombauer and Holmes hold that a real concept was weakened by Moltke's changes and the August detachments, which leaves open how close it came.[^mombauer-2001] The branch renders the argument so the checklist can be read against the map.

feasibility.condition: No corps leave the right wing for East Prussia
feasibility.note: The Guard Reserve and XI Corps entrained for the east on 25–26 August, two days before Tannenberg made them unnecessary; Moltke later called it his worst mistake.

feasibility.condition: No corps are left behind to mask Antwerp, Maubeuge and Givet
feasibility.note: The III Reserve Corps stayed before Antwerp from 20 August, the VII Reserve Corps at Maubeuge until 7 September; the IX Reserve Corps reached the front only at the end of the month.

feasibility.condition: Belgian railways, bridges and tunnels are captured intact and the armies are supplied beyond the railheads
feasibility.note: Demolitions and the fight for Liège kept the railheads days behind the marching corps; by the Marne the 1st Army was living off the country.

feasibility.condition: The 1st Army passes west of Paris instead of wheeling inside it
feasibility.note: On 30–31 August Kluck turned south-east to roll up the French left and keep touch with Bülow — with Moltke's approval on 2 September.

feasibility.condition: The French do not redeploy west by rail in time to form a new army at Paris
feasibility.note: Joffre's Instruction générale no 2 of 25 August built the 6th Army at Amiens and then Paris from corps railed out of Lorraine and Alsace; it struck Kluck's flank on 5 September.

feasibility.condition: The French armies stand and are caught rather than retreating out of the pocket
feasibility.note: Joffre gave ground for a fortnight and kept the armies intact; a pocket closes only on an enemy that stays to be enclosed.

feasibility.condition: The right wing marches faster and farther than the historical 1st Army did
feasibility.note: Kluck's corps averaged some 30 kilometres a day for a fortnight to reach the Marne; the wheel west of Paris adds a hundred kilometres or more to the same timetable, on the same legs.
